newsitem.title: LAOS: Laos, developers say NT2 dam on economic target.
newsitem.headline: Laos, developers say NT2 dam on economic target.

text.p: Laos' largest planned hydroelectric dam, Nam Theun 2 (NT2), remains economically viable despite a downturn in the neighbouring Thai market that will take the bulk of its power output, officials say.

But preliminary talks with the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand (EGAT) have resulted in the lowering of the dam's planned capacity from 900 megawatts to 681 megawatts, said David Iverach, director of the Nam Theun II Electricity Consortium (NTEC) in an interview on Saturday.

NTEC, which includes Transfield Corp, Electricite de France, Italian Thai Development Plc, Thailand's Jasmine International Plc and Phatra Thanakit Co Ltd hopes to develop the $1.5 billion project with most of the power going to Thailand.

The NT2 is a build-own-operate-transfer project developed by NTEC, with 75 percent, and the Lao government, 25 percent. Laos will gain 100 percent ownership of the project after 25 years of operation.
Iverach said EGAT had indicated that it viewed NT2 mainly as a solid baseload supply and had thus offered tariffs that did not justify the larger 900 megawatt supply.
That conclusion remains subject to change, however, pending completion of a study into alternative designs and future negotiations over tariffs, he said.

The NT2, about 250 km (155 miles) east of Vientiane, is located in and around the Nakai Plateau. To the northeast of the plateau are mountains which form the main catchment area for a 450-square-km proposed reservoir.
The dam, which will be located across the Nam Theun, the Theun River, at the northwest end of the plateau, will be about 45 metres high and 325 metres long, according to NTEC.
Its reservoir will store 3.5 billion cubic metres of water, which will flow down a tunnel to a powerhouse at the base of an escarpment more than 350 metres below the reservoir level.

The powerhouse will have four turbines -- three in operation and one spare. Twin 230 kV transmission lines will carry the electricity 140 km to Thailand, where it will enter the Thai tranmission grid.
Iverach and Lao officials at a public hearing on the dam said they are confident that EGAT would buy power from NT2.

The Lao government said that Thailand, with its 13 percent growth in energy demand, was expected to absorb virtually all of the power from several planned hydroelectric dams despite a recent economic slump and plans to conserve electricity.
Under a June 1996 agreement, EGAT agreed to purchase 3,000 megawatts from Laos by 2006.

But Iverach said a key financial uncertainty remains. That is the $100 million loan guarantees from the World Bank that are contingent on studies on the dam's impact and a series of public hearings on the project.
NTEC has said it will pull out of the project unless it gets the guarantees, considered critical because 70 percent of the funds needed to develop NT2 will be borrowed from international lenders.
NTEC has also asked for direct loans from the International Finance Corporation, but no decision has been made.
